title: Slice-and-Stitch multi-GPU playbook
body:
Goal:
This is a practical design/playbook for a "slice-and-stitch" approach to multi-GPU inference serving. The objective is to support high-throughput, low-latency generation for large models by splitting tensors across devices (tensor-slicing), performing local kernel execution, and stitching partial outputs with tuned inter-GPU communication. This doc focuses on runtime behavior (scheduling, kernel selection, KV cache ownership), communication patterns (ring vs tree vs pairwise), and operational heuristics for production rollout.

Context / motivation:
- Existing approaches either replicate full model weights per GPU (easy but memory-inefficient) or rely on heavy-handed pipeline/tensor-parallel toolchains that assume static batch profiles. We need a runtime that:
  - adapts to mixed incoming request sizes (1-8 tokens hot, long-context cold)
  - minimizes cross-GPU traffic for short-latency requests
  - retains ability to scale for high throughput batches
- "Slice-and-stitch" aims to be a middle ground: slice the heavy operations (matmul/attention) across GPUs at the tensor level when beneficial, otherwise fall back to single-device execution. Stitch partial token logits/kv shards back together with minimal synchronization.

High-level design:
1) Slicing model compute:
   - Partition strategies: row-wise, column-wise, and attention-head partitioning. Default initial strategy: row-wise weight-slicing for linear layers and KV projection to preserve softmax semantics with minimal additional allreduce cost.
   - Slice metadata: For every model op the planner keeps an immutable slice descriptor (device_count, slice_offsets, expected message sizes).

2) Micro-batching & micro-stitch: non-blocking stitching
   - Micro-batcher groups requests with similar required device partitioning (same sequence length bucket and same model variant) and issues slices concurrently.
   - Each GPU computes its partial logits and partial KV updates; a small "stitch RPC" gathers partial logits for final softmax and sampling. We aim for a non-blocking gather: start softmax on the local GPU for its shard while receiving remote shards progressively and merge increments.

3) Communication topology (practical defaults for production):
   - Local single-host multi-GPU: use ring-optimized NCCL collectives for large slices; for many small messages use pairwise CUDA IPC + shared CUDA streams to reduce NCCL overhead.
   - Multi-host: prefer hierarchical ring (intra-host rings + inter-host tree) to reduce cross-host tail latency; maintain async progress threads to ensure small messages are forwarded immediately.
   - Fallback: if NCCL startup/collective latency dominates for tiny messages, revert to an RPC-stitch path over gRPC/UCX for that micro-batch.

4) KV cache ownership & coherence:
   - Sharded KV store: prefer ownership-by-slice (each GPU stores the KV rows it computed). For attention, this minimizes KV broadcast.
   - Consistency model: eventual per-request consistency with causal guarantees (i.e., a request sees the KV cache mutations produced by earlier steps of the same request).
   - Eviction/aging: LRU per-shard with a global policy manager that can reassign hot keys (tokens) to GPUs for locality. Reassignments must be logged and have a versioned manifest.

5) Scheduler and placement heuristics:
   - Cost model: estimated token-ops and comm-size estimate -> score devices by predicted end-to-end latency.
   - Heuristics: small requests (<32 tokens, single-shot) -> prefer single-GPU pinned execution to avoid comm setup. Medium requests (32-256 tokens) -> try 2-way slice split. Large requests/batches -> scale slices to maximize throughput.
   - Concurrency model: allow N inflight micro-batches per device where N is derived from GPU mem footprint + kernel concurrency. Aggressive packing under high throughput.

6) Kernel selection & autotuning:
   - Per-slice kernel catalog mapping: quantization bitwidth, fused attention kernels, and matmul tiling parameters.
   - Warm-start autotuner: collect microbenchmarks in prod dark traffic to choose per-op kernels by slice size distribution.

Operational concerns and tradeoffs:
- Latency vs cost: slicing reduces memory pressure and can lower cost for large-models, but small requests may suffer from comm overhead. Auto-fallback thresholds are crucial (empirically measured).
- Determinism: stitch ordering and partial-softmax numerics must be consistent across topologies; provide a deterministic mode for QA/regression testing that forces single-device or ordered gather.
- Fault tolerance: if a GPU fails mid-request, switch to degraded path: reassemble remaining slices and route to a warm spare or single-device fallback. Maintain request-level timeouts and graceful degradation (partial response with a warning header).
- Security: KV shards contain unencrypted prompt state; ensure KMS/enclave protections on private deployments and in-transit encryption for cross-host transfers.

Experiments to run (priority ordering):
1) Microbench: 1k variations of shard sizes (128-4096 row splits) measuring per-step latency, NCCL startup, and payload cost.
2) Tiny-message path: compare NCCL-allreduce vs CUDA-IPC vs UCX-RPC for 256B-16KB messages.
3) KV locality: synthetic workload with 80/20 hot tokens to test reassignment policy overhead vs benefit.
4) Failure injection: GPU removal mid-inflight, measure tail latency and SLA compliance.

Metric definitions (so infra can instrument consistently):
- slice_serialize_ms: time to prepare slice buffer for comm (host staging, pinned mem)
- inter_gpu_bytes: total bytes transferred per request across GPUs
- stitch_p99_ms: 99th percentile time between last local partial computed and final stitched logits ready
- kv_remote_hit_rate: fraction of KV accesses satisfied locally vs requiring remote fetch
- fallback_rate: fraction of requests that were routed to single-device fallback due to comm/timeout

Open questions / trade-offs to discuss:
- Should we support head-based slicing (split by attention heads) as a first-class strategy? Pros: lower comm for attention; Cons: more complex kernel bookkeeping and potential softmax distortion.
- Dynamic ownership rebalancing frequency: continuous small moves vs batched reassignments.
- How to integrate with existing decay/cache features in Optimize (pin hot prompt prefixes at higher priority)?

Short-term action items (next 8 weeks):
- [ ] Implement a prototype slice descriptor and planner in runtime core (Priya, Ethan)
- [ ] Microbench harness for intra-host tiny-message NCCL vs IPC (Marisol)
- [ ] KV shard manifest format and eviction stub (Theo)
- [ ] Add metrics hooks: slice_serialize_ms, stitch_p99_ms, kv_remote_hit_rate (instrumentation task)
- [ ] Draft a small internal playbook for on-call about fallback behavior and how to triage slice-related incidents

Appendix: quick play examples (textual)
- Example 1: single 16-token request to 8B model:
  Decision: single-GPU execution (threshold single-device), latency path used.
- Example 2: batch of 64 short requests (8 tokens each) arriving in burst:
  Decision: microbatch into 8x8 groups, 2-way slice splitting to keep per-device mem <85% and achieve 2x throughput increase. Use ring gather for logits.
- Example 3: long single generation, 1024 tokens:
  Decision: pipeline the steps, keep KV sharded by slice owner. Periodically checkpoint KV manifest to control reassignment costs.

Notes to self / rough ideas for follow-ups:
- Explore compile-time helpers that emit stitch kernels (small fused reduction kernels) to avoid host-side gathers for common slice patterns.
- Consider a tiny persistent local broker per-host that aggregates partial logits for micro-batches to reduce the number of point-to-point transfers.

References:
- internal: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/issues/712 (baseline tensor-slicing sketches)
- literature: "ZeRO-Inference" variants for sharded KV behavior; recent preprints on attention-head partitioning for inference.

This is intentionally a working doc: rough, experimental, and meant to capture heuristics and initial experiment suites. Feedback welcome; will iterate after first round of microbench results.
